name: Codium fragile seaweed
lede: Codium fragile seaweed is ColorHub's name for Miru-iro (海松色), a traditional Japanese color named for a spongy green seaweed also called dead man's fingers.

sections.title: Miru-iro, a seaweed's color
sections.body:
The Wikipedia survey "Traditional colors of Japan" lists this color under the romanized name Miru-iro, written 海松色 [1]. 海松 names *Codium fragile*, a spongy, branching green seaweed also called dead man's fingers in English, and 色 is simply "color"; the library's gloss keeps the biological name intact as "Codium fragile seaweed color" [1]. No book consulted here independently confirms a date for the name [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[dusty-brown]], [[bronze-lustre]], [[gull]] and [[japanese-bush-warbler]], at 3.5, 4.3, 5.3 and 5.4 ΔE [1]. The hex, #524B2A, is a modern screen approximation, not a measurement of dried or living seaweed [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within range of this swatch is one of the most common in our archive: it appears in 3,151 of the 23,781 paintings, about 13.25 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it 2,073 times [2]. That makes it more common than 96 percent of the named colors we track [2].

It peaks in the 1700s, present in 422 of 3,449 paintings from that century, 1.4 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in just over a third of the paintings that carry it [2]. Shibata Zeshin is its most devoted painter, using it in 9 of his 15 works here, well above his museums' baseline rate [2]. The earliest dated appearance we have is 1100, though the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a true first sighting; it also shares canvases with Dark Citrine and Dull Citrine more often than chance would predict [2].

openers: Codium fragile seaweed is named for a real, branching green alga, and it is one of the most common colors in our painting archive.

issues: No book-level source for the name's history beyond the library gloss; stated as undocumented rather than guessed.
Umber given as nearest common English name but flagged as a loose match (dE 13.7), with dusty-brown noted as the closer library suggestion.
